guides.title: Fix 'The NTFS Partition is in an Unsafe State' in Dual Boot
guides.symptom: Linux refuses to mount Windows partition with error: 'Windows is hibernated, refused to mount' or 'Unsafe state'
guides.description: Disable Windows Fast Startup and clean up the hibernation metadata locking your hard drive from cross-boot mounting.
causes: Windows 'Fast Startup' feature puts the computer into a hybrid hibernation (saving kernel state to `hiberfil.sys`) instead of performing a clean shutdown
Linux detects the active hibernation flag and locks the partition to prevent catastrophic filesystem corruption
guides.whyItWorks: When Fast Startup is enabled, Windows does not unmount the NTFS filesystem. If Linux were to write files to it, Windows would overwrite those changes upon waking up. Disabling Fast Startup ensures a true unmount with an empty journal.

steps.instruction: Disable Fast Startup in Windows Control Panel
steps.detail:
1. Boot into Windows.
2. Press Win+R, type `powercfg.cpl` and press Enter.
3. In the left sidebar, click 'Choose what the power buttons do'.
4. Click the blue shield link: 'Change settings that are currently unavailable'.
5. Scroll down to 'Shutdown settings' and UNCHECK 'Turn on fast startup (recommended)'.
6. Click 'Save changes'.

steps.instruction: Completely turn off Windows Hibernation via Command Prompt
steps.detail:
Open Command Prompt as Administrator in Windows and run:
powercfg /h off
This deletes `hiberfil.sys` and guarantees that every Windows shutdown is 100% clean, freeing up 8GB-32GB of disk space.

If you are currently locked in Linux and need urgent access to a file on the Windows drive, you can mount it in read-only mode safely:
sudo mount -o ro /dev/nvme0n1p3 /mnt/windows
(Replace with your Windows partition). Read-only mode will not corrupt the hibernated filesystem.

guides.title: Changing Default Boot OS & Boot Order (GRUB & efibootmgr)
guides.symptom: Computer boots into Linux when I want Windows as default, or GRUB menu timeout is too long/short
guides.description: Configure GRUB default entry, remember the last booted OS, and reorder hardware UEFI boot targets using `efibootmgr`.
keywords: boot windows by default dual boot
causes: GRUB default setting configured to entry 0 (Linux kernel)
UEFI NVRAM boot order having Linux as first priority entry
guides.whyItWorks: GRUB configuration file `/etc/default/grub` controls menu display timeouts and default choice indices. Alternatively, modifying the motherboard's NVRAM via `efibootmgr` dictates which bootloader EFI firmware loads before GRUB even starts.

steps.detail:
In Linux, open terminal and edit GRUB settings:
sudo nano /etc/default/grub
Find `GRUB_DEFAULT=0`. You can change it to:
`GRUB_DEFAULT=saved`
And add this line directly underneath:
`GRUB_SAVEDEFAULT=true`
This makes GRUB remember whichever OS you booted last time! To change timeout (seconds), edit `GRUB_TIMEOUT=5`.

steps.instruction: Apply and compile the new GRUB configuration
steps.detail:
Run:
sudo update-grub
On Fedora/Arch: `sudo grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg`.
Reboot to test your new default.

steps.instruction: Change hardware UEFI boot order with `efibootmgr`
steps.detail:
Inspect your motherboard's UEFI boot order list in Linux:
sudo efibootmgr
You will see entries like:
`Boot0001* Windows Boot Manager`
`Boot0002* ubuntu`
`BootOrder: 0002,0001`
To make Windows Boot Manager boot first directly:
sudo efibootmgr -o 0001,0002

guides.title: Fixing BitLocker Recovery Key Prompt on Every Dual Boot
guides.symptom: Every time I choose Windows after using Linux, Windows asks for a 48-digit BitLocker recovery key
guides.description: Prevent TPM PCR measurement mismatch between Windows and GRUB so BitLocker boots smoothly without prompts.
causes: The TPM (Trusted Platform Module) measures the boot chain (PCR 7). When booting through GRUB instead of directly through Windows Boot Manager, the TPM considers the bootloader altered and seals the BitLocker decryption key
guides.whyItWorks: Suspending BitLocker protection for one reboot cycle allows the TPM to record the new GRUB boot chain measurements into its PCR registers. Alternatively, choosing Windows directly via UEFI F12 boot menu bypasses GRUB's alteration of PCR 7.

steps.detail: Log in to your Microsoft Account from another device at: https://account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey. Enter the 48-digit numerical key on your PC to boot into Windows.

steps.instruction: Suspend BitLocker protection to recalibrate TPM
steps.detail:
In Windows, open Command Prompt as Administrator and run:
manage-bde -protectors -disable C:
Restart your PC and boot into Linux once. Then reboot back into Windows (it will boot without asking for the key). In Windows, re-enable protection:
manage-bde -protectors -enable C:
This seals the key against the dual-boot environment.

steps.instruction: Best practice: Use F12 hardware boot menu for BitLocker
steps.detail: If your company or school strictly enforces BitLocker PCR 7 validation, configure your PC to boot Windows Boot Manager by default, and simply tap F12 (or your motherboard boot key) whenever you want to boot into Linux. This prevents GRUB from touching the TPM when loading Windows.
